Challengers Card Game | Strategy/Interactive Deck Management Game | Fun Family Game for Adults and Kids | Ages 10+ | 1-8 Players | Average Playtime 45 Minutes | Made by Z-Man Games For this game, you really need to know what you're getting.

This is a strategy deckbuilding game with a lot of silly, and a little stupid. And if you're OK with a lot of silly and a little stupid, you will probably love Challengers! if you have a even number of players.

In Challengers, you are deckbuilding in preparation for a game of War. Yes, that game of War where you mindlessly turn over cards and hope for high numbers, even knowing that there are a bunch of low numbers in your deck.

The only player choice is made during the deckbuilding phase, and then you get to sit back and watch the chaos.

And if you're OK with a chaotic game like this, where choices are limited and it's all down to luck, then you've found a winner with Challengers! If you think this sounds like a waste of time, then for you, it probably is. We had a few stand up and cheer come-from-behind moments and a lot of inglorious losses.

This is a great deckbuilding intro for kids, and for the grownups with the right tastes, this will be a hit, but I think a lot of people will absolutely hate it also.
text_fidelity_b: Challengers Card Game | Strategy/Interactive Deck Management Game | Fun Family Game for Adults and Kids | Ages 10+ | 1-8 Players | Average Playtime 45 Minutes | Made by Z-Man Games

text_fidelity_a:
WowWee - MiP the Toy Robot - White This is a four star product in many ways. But I'm giving it three due to the following factors...

Excellent build quality and hardware features. However, without some additional software and accessories this you won't see lasting use.

Hardware: you WILL need a phone or tablet to unlock the limited potential of this toy. The included gesture and sound functionality is too rudimentary (and yet also hard to acess consistently) for lasting interest. If you don't plan to provide access to a tablet or phone, get WowWee's robotic dog product instead. Although it is easy to set up an obstacle course or seesaw on your own, purpose-built accessories would go a long way towards providing a "fiction" for the toy to inhabit, as well as proven fun activities.

Software: the existing apps are very well made and provide a significant boost to the toys functionality. I'd say about 75%. However, most are of limited scope and soon become repetitive. The best feature is the ability to remotely drive the robot and also record its adventures. I'd like to see a feature that allows kids to rudimentarily program the robot (perhaps to interact with purpose built accessories) not just activate sounds and colored lights... I'd also like to see the toolset opened to adults (Lua scripting?) so that they can extend the functionality for Pre-K through K STEM learning.

I understand trying to hit price points is important. But this is either a $75 toy with a few $25 accessory kits, or a $125 toy all in. The existing package (while decent) is limiting the potential of the product.
text_fidelity_b: WowWee - MiP the Toy Robot - White

text_fidelity_a:
Monopoly Empire Game "Monopoly Empire" is like a simplified version of the traditional game of Monopoly. The colors and layout of the board are very similar to the traditional game, but each has a famous logo, such as Hasbro or EA Sports, instead of street names. The object of the game is to add tiles with various brands to your Times Square type "billboard tower" before the other players. The more brands you add to your billboard, the more money you get when passing Go, which allows you to buy more brands. The game tokens are representative of the brands in the game, such as a bottle of Coca-Cola and an Xbox controller. The board is a bit smaller than the traditional board, because it doesn't have railroads.

The game is easy to learn, in part because of an excellent, full-color instruction guide that includes a very clear diagram of how to set up the board. The way the items are priced make it easy to pay for purchased tiles. Although the game is lacking the excitement and strategy of trading properties and building houses as in the original version of Monopoly, it is good for a quick game. It would be easy for kids to learn and play. The game is most fun when it's a close race between the players to complete their towers. If one player takes a large, early lead, it's hard for the other person to come from behind.

Note: The logoed tiles have various sizes, which is part of the game. However, the sometimes the positioning of the stickers with the logo make it confusing to put them into the tower correctly.

All in all, this is a good game that is easy to play and goes by quickly.
text_fidelity_b: Monopoly Empire Game

FurReal Friends Pax My Poopin Pup Plush Toy (Amazon Exclusive) I had high hopes for this little pooping doggo.. I purchased as a Christmas gift for my daughter (3 years old), who was obsessed with walking our dog and watching him pop (she’s a weirdo). Overall, she has gotten a fair amount of play and enjoyment out of the little fella, so I would *probably* purchase again.

Pros: He makes cute little doggy noises, he’s has soft fur.

Cons: He was much smaller than I expected (but my fault, as size is objective). He was overall much harder than I expected (other than his thin layer of fuzzy fur coat, he’s completely hard to the squeeze). He has wheels (which for some reason I thought he was more automatic than that). The leash is short (it was the perfect size for my tiny 3 year old when we bought it, but our 4 year old friend had to bend over to push it around). The treats / poo pellets are incredibly small. We lost a couple on christmas when we opened the gift.. and then a few more since. We have less than half left now (which I think is an accomplishment since we’ve had it almost a year!).

My toddler and her friends have enjoyed playing with it, but they have 1) been hurt by his hard material build (just minor boo boo, but still) 2) tried to eat the teeny pellet foods (cause, why not?) and 3) shoved other objects in its mouth that they weren’t supposed to. The design concept isn’t bad, but I do wish it was slightly bigger, with slightly bigger treats, a slightly longer leash, slightly more “squeezable”... you catch my drift. And with all that in mind, I probably would have gone with a different puppers.

Moorebot Scout - Tiny AI Camera Robot for Tech-Minded, Pets/Edlerly Watching/Security/Smart Home/Crawlspace Inspection, 1080P, Auto Patrol, Nightvision, Track Option, Indoor (2023) My office was just moved to a new building that as yet has no cameras inside...Well...Sort of. Now I've got Scout here to take care of business. It's like a Ring doorbell on wheels.

I'm having a lot of fun controlling it manually from home. It connects to the wifi at work and I check in on things using the app. It's working very well and seems to hold a signal about 250kbps. 1080p recordings look fine. For myself, the night vision works a charm. It's clear enough to identify people, and that's all that matters. Plus, driving it around my office while I'm in bed is pretty cool, too.

Battery takes about three hours to charge out of the box and it lasts about 2hr running around the building before it goes back to the base. Most recent firmware update makes that process significantly faster, too. If you've got it on a slick surface, it might have some trouble, but it'll get plugged in eventually. Says battery runs out after an hour using only night vision, but you can set that to automatic in the app.

Around the house, the little noises are kinda neat, but for use as security, that'd be something to disable....except the alarm. That's something to keep on in case you need to scare someone off. Recording all that stuff and saving files to the phone is a plus.

I really like this little guy. It's definitely something you'll have to play around with, but it is a load of fun getting set up.

text_fidelity_a:
LeapFrog LeapTV Dance and Learn Educational, Active Video Game I received this game through the Amazon Vine Program, although the usual green writing may not be written above.

This game is pretty good if your kid is young enough to get excited over "dancing" to burn off energy. There are a bunch of mini games to do alone or with friends that require body movement to excel at.

The deal with the lighting is this, and it applies to all the camera based games: if you have low light, the camera may not register your hand is moving in front of something that is dark, and therefore will not pick up on the movement. So, for example, when I am using ambient light and the living room is not bright, my red couch looks almost black on the screen, so if you have to touch something that is in that area, it won't pick up on it. Similarly, if you turn on the lights, those items will be picked up automatically. Add light or put a white sheet on the couch, in that case.

text_fidelity_a:
Monopoly Empire Game [[VIDEOID:8f653ee987e2df8b52e209e097da8a22]] This is such a cool game! It's a scaled down version of Monopoly, and each game only takes 5-15 minutes to play, instead of the hours of a regular Monopoly game. So you'll hear something with this Monopoly game that you won't hear with any other Monopoly game, which is "Want to play again?"

It still captures the essence of Monopoly, so it still feels like a Monopoly game. It's more of a social game than a strategy game, but that will make it more fun for more people.

They've taken out the property cards, and replaced them with little tiles and a tower. The number of tiles, not the original value of the tile, determine how much that you pay when you land on someone else's property. The old Community Chest cards are now Empire cards, and you get a couple to hold on to at the start of the game, and you can use these strategically, and do various combos with them.

It's very fun, and I liked it a lot. If you get just one game this year, this should be the game you pick.

Pros:
+Excellent instructions
+Extremely well designed
+Has cool brands like Fender, Nerf, and Coke
+Quick version of Monopoly (I never thought I'd ever use quick and Monopoly in the same sentence.)
+They did an awesome job of play testing this game. It's very balanced and very fun. Whoever worked on the team that made this game should be promoted.

Cons:
-Less strategy than regular Monopoly, but it is more fun for more people
-Because it's subsidized by advertising, they really should be giving this game away. But, the advertising isn't as annoying as in other games.
text_fidelity_b: Monopoly Empire Game

text_fidelity_a:
Hasbro Gaming Sorry Spin My family has really enjoyed playing this updated version of an old favorite. The basic rules are the same as in the original Sorry! Each player has four pawns to move around the board from Start to Home. You draw a card to find out how many spaces you can move your game piece. Landing on another player's pawn sends them back to start as does the Sorry! card, just as in the classic version.

What's different about Sorry Spin is the spinning board. The center circle is the main board, with connecting circles for each color's home which fit together like gears. The challenge of the spinning board is your home is contantly changing position in relation to the main board. You may be just a few spaces away from reaching your home track when the board will spin and you will end up all the way across the board from your home.

It took about 5 minutes to assemble the game board, which seems very sturdy. We had some trouble spinning the board on a slick surface (wood table, counter top), but when we placed it on a placemat, it worked fine. A nice addition is a box that can be assembled and used to store the cards.

This is a great family game which is faster paced than the original version of the game due to the spinning board and a shorter path between start and home. Also any number gets a pawn out of start. (unlike the original which requires a 1 or 2). Older kids and adults will enjoy the suggested variation of the two-player game in which each person selects two different colors instead of only one.
text_fidelity_b: Hasbro Gaming Sorry Spin

The LED lights are amazing and it was easy to watch in the dark at night, or just to enjoy during the day.

The "battery" is very different, you have to hook it up to the black device which has an USB and you need your own adapter to plug and recharge it. Each use lasts maybe 10 minutes max before you need to change batteries and recharge the first one. It is a great way to teach your child to take on different perspectives--if the drone is facing you, your left is actually its' right and your right is it's left. You have to consider that when using the controller just like with RC cars, except it is hard to tell from up in the air. You have to press left or right slightly to figure out which side then rotate it around so you can drive it. It comes with replacement spinners and a small screwdriver.

The return mode is nice, if you are freaking out and afraid it will go into a tree and unable to figure out which way to turn, just press that return button and it will come back to you.

Cons:
1. The drone was able to flip on the first day, but afterwards, for whatever reason, that stopped working. That didn't stop my son from enjoying it.
2. The video/camera app did not work on my phone. I tried different ways to get it to work.
3. Less than a week later, two of the "arms" that connect the ring to the base broke so now it won't lift up correctly. Even with superglue, that didn't help. Unfortunately, it is made of cheap flexible plastic.

So bottom line, I would not recommend buying this item.

This drone is Made in China and being sold by a Chinese company on Amazon.

text_fidelity_a:
Chutes and Ladders Board Game Like many of us over 40, we grew up with this game and recognize the graphics of the Classic Chutes and Ladders Board Game. Recently, after my dad passed, we cleared out our old house and found my old game. It followed my brother home to his family, but now I'm curious to compare the two.

Outside of nostalgia, the question is if the game stands on its own in 2015. My four year-old boy thinks so. He doesn't care about 1972 (or even know it existed, as time began with him, as he sees it). He begs to play it, right along with Trouble! and Legos.

Essentially, there's no strategy. The person going version has a small chance of winning, but for all intents and purposes, it is pure chance.

To move forward, the player spins from 1-6. Whatever square he might land on is either neutral, a ladder or a slide. Slides move him back to an earlier square, ladders move him up, and neutral squares allow him to stay put until the next move. There is no decision making.

Is it fun? Very much so, according to my boy. As there are 100 squares, there are plenty of opportunities to climb ladders and slide down. It is a little tricky to follow which direction to go, as the numbers start left-to-right, but zig-zag at each end. A patient older child or adult needs to be on-hand to help with game play.

Anthony Trendl
anthonytrendl.com
text_fidelity_b: Chutes and Ladders Board Game

ThinkFun and Crazy Aaron's Thinking Putty Puzzle and STEM Toy for Boys and Girls Ages 8 and Up - The Famous Thinking Putty in Logic Game Form I’ve played many of Thinkfun’s logic puzzles, and use them in my classroom. So, I was very interested in their new logic puzzle that uses Crazy Aaron’s Putty. This game has some similarities with their other logic puzzles. It comes with 60 cards that show the challenge setup on one side and a possible answer on the back. The setup for each challenge takes the longest than any other logic puzzle because you have to tear the balls of putty off each color. It is challenging, even the first few challenges’ solutions aren’t immediately visible, they take some thought to solve.

I enjoyed this for myself and found it relaxing to put together and solve. I could see some kids not having the patience to play through the puzzle. I don’t plan to use this one in my classroom because I think the putty would get funky after having some kids play with it, and there could be some putty mixing that intentionally or unintentionally could happen and ruin the game.

Overall, this is a very clever idea. I’ve played the beginning challenges and enjoyed figuring them out. Kids will love the putty, but I’m not sure how long the challenges will hold their attention.

text_fidelity_a:
HUBSAN X4 H107C HD 2MP Camera 2.4G 4CH 6 Axis Gyro RC Quadcopter Red/White (PH-H107C) At first I received the SD version instead of the HD version from one seller on Amazon. I returned it.The Little One's Choice got it right and sent me the HD version for which I had paid. Make sure you get what you paid for. It should say "HD Camera" in big letters on the Hubsan box. Unfortunately, the correct one they sent had horrible very dark lines in the video in all types of lighting conditions. I had to return it. The replacement was fine.

My "review" is going to be a bit rambling from an experienced guy to those who are tying to get started in this hobby. My hope is that I might have something to say that the old-timers might find useful as well.

My short review in this paragraph is that this quad is awesome (overused word, I know, but it fits here) for the price and simply amazing. I've had hours of fun with mine and I own 2 other non-camera Hubsans, one Proto-X and a Blade Quad Nano. This Hubsan quad is the most bang for the buck. I've also got big copters that are gathering dust while I have fun with these small ones. Strangely, I'm not missing them. Did I mention these little things are fun?

It is refreshing to the point of joyfulness to be able to fly this quad around since it is so relatively inexpensive and nimble. I bought several bags of props out of an abundance of caution and have not used one yet. Still, I don't crash much, so if you are new at this, you might need more propellers than the one set provided. I bought some spare batteries (they are blue, sold in a set of 5) and a couple of the Traxxas 2-port chargers. These work fine and let you have more charged batteries handy.

I want to say this quad is easy to fly. For me it is very easy, but it is also fun. I understand that for those who have never flown any type of RC rotor craft that you will have to be serious about learning to use and fly this little thing properly.

Don't be frustrated if you crash a lot at first. Fly in an open area outdoors if possible. If you fly indoors, which I know is a very attractive prospect at first, you will crash into walls and ceiling often and perhaps lose some propellers. At first you may even forget which hand "does what" and crash pretty hard. The body of this quad is tough, but I have seen some photos of broken ones. All of those slammed hard onto concrete walls or slabs.

If a crash is imminent, learn to cut the power immediately. Throttle off completely. You do not want the motors stalling against an obstruction. They will burn out if you abuse them that way. Also, never try to bump the throttle to kick the motors on in an attempt to flip the copter upright if it sets down at an angle. Motivate your body to the quad, pick it up and set it down straight. It will last longer that way.

The rotor guard is taped to the bottom of the tray. Use it if you are unsure of your skills. By the way, when removing the props to put this on, do be sure to hold down the motor body. If it comes up too far the motor wires will snap off. It is only held in place with friction. Use a pinching grasp to pull the prop off. There's a little wrench to help with pulling the props. Use that if one came with your quad. Some people don't get one, I don't know why.

This same type of grasp is also the correct way to disconnect the battery. If you pull by the wires, you will soon have a broken connection. Try to grasp both sides of the connector with your thumbs while you squeeze to persuade the connector away from its mate. Try to make contact with as much connector, not wire, as possible.

There are many videos on YouTube which are instructive for newbies. Especially helpful even for an experienced guy like me was one video that showed how to restore a stuck motor to working condition with a pair of pliers. Especially learn how to reset the gyros with the transmitter and how to zero-out the transmitter itself. Read the instructions carefully and you'll see that you can adjust the sensitivity of the transmitter relative to control input. Learn and understand how to use the trim buttons. There is a lot of info in that little manual. It's not the greatest manual I've seen, but it is a good effort at one and most of the hazy parts are cleared up on YouTube.

I've found that when the lights flash during flight to signal a low battery (time to land!) that the voltage is about 3.7 volts. This is a pretty safe voltage for storing a LiPo so if you are not going to fly again soon don't bother to charge it. Letting a fully charged LiPo sit for more than a week can be hard on it. Take good care of the battery by never flying it to the point where it is dead. In fact, as soon as you get the flashing warning - land! If you are flying outside where you can't see the warning well in daylight, I'd recommend setting a kitchen timer set to 5-1/2 minutes and timing your flights. Better safe than sorry. Once you run a LiPo down too far it's gone or soon will be.

If you have spare batteries all charged up during a flying session, avoid the temptation of replacing an exhausted battery with a fresh one and getting right back up into the air. My opinion is you should let the motors cool down for a few minutes first. They will be very hot after you complete a full flight so give them a chance to cool a bit before you take to the skies again.

They sell higher capacity batteries here on Amazon. I believe they are 500 mAh. I would not recommend them. Any longer flight time potential will be offset by the extra battery weight. Also the motors will have to work harder at higher RPM to keep the quad airborne. I think the stock capacity battery size is well-suited to this quad.

The instructions encourage you to stuff the battery leads up into the copter body so they don't hang out. I just let them hang out. Stuffing them up in there just stresses all the connections and solder joints and the wires don't stay up in there very will anyway. Just my opinion on that one, folks.

The motors are amazing on these little quads. They are good for about 70 hours of actual flying time. That's really pretty good. Still, if you are going to use the quad a lot and put about 100 flights on it, you will eventually have a motor go bad. It is a good idea to have a spaare motor kit. The motors on the 107C are 8.5mm wide. The motors from the 107L will NOT fit. So get the correct ones.

If you have to replace a motor, you'll have to be able to solder or know somebody who can do it for you. It's a simple soldering task for an experienced RC hobbyist so members of that ilk will have no problem. If you are just leaping into RC with this quad and don't have those skills because you haven't had to suffer the school of hard knocks like we old-timers did, you just have to learn soldering or lean on somebody who can do it for you. Some solder and a basic pencil soldering iron can be obtained for less that 20 bucks if you want to learn a new, useful skill.

As for the HD camera, it is quite sufficient. This little camera will never be super stable outdoors in wind but the video is still quite good. In windy conditions, you MUST press down the right stick to get into expert mode. If you don't you will not have sufficient control movement to fight the wind. You will watch helplessly as your copter drifts away from you if you can't bring it down immediately. Incidentally, while in expert mode if you are afraid of flipping the copter because of the unlimited control movement it provides, just click the left stick down to enter "no-flip" mode.

Also regarding the camera, you must follow the correct procedure to obtain video. Turn on your transmitter with the throttle completely off. Insert the SD card. Connect the battery. Wait for the red light to turn off in the SD card slot. All you should see is a tiny blue light (NO red light). Now you can press the little switch on the side to start recording. You'll see the tiny red light flashing. When you finish your video flight, you must press the little switch again to stop the video. Wait for the red light to go out (indicating the video file has been saved. Now you may unplug the battery. If desired you may also unplug the SD card now.

If you don't use the switch to stop the video, or if you unplug the battery while the red light is flashing, you will save no video.

Always plug/unplug the SD card with the battery disconnected! Also, the SD card socket is not like those on many mobile phones with which you may be familiar. There is no "spring action". You just slide the card in until it bottoms in the slot. If you keep pushing it when you feel resistance thinking you are going to push against the locking spring, don't do it. Push too hard and you could harm the card socket. So go easy on it!

It is amazing that we can now buy a gyro-stabilized copter and get it hovering with so little "learning". It was not unusual for people to spend weeks just learning the touch to get a single rotor copter off the ground in one piece and into a hover. Now it is so much cheaper and simpler. I won't say easy, because as I have said if you are absolute noob you have to learn the controls and develop your skills. Still, you should be able to get it off the ground and hover without too much agony.

If you are interested in flying RC, I don't think you can go wrong with giving this quad a try. I feel it is a bargain price and rewarding and fun to learn to fly.
text_fidelity_b: HUBSAN X4 H107C HD 2MP Camera 2.4G 4CH 6 Axis Gyro RC Quadcopter Red/White (PH-H107C)

text_fidelity_a: Doggie Doo Corgi Game - Unpredictable Action - Feed The Doggie and Collect His Doo to Win - Includes 24-Piece Puzzle by Goliath This type of thing isn't usually my cup of tea and I typically dislike potty humor. This looked like something to bring humor on the days that my guys aren't getting along, though. It is on the weird side(even thought so from my 3 boys), with all the noises, but it is also on the humorous side. To play, you stick a bit of slime("food") into the bone. The players take turns rolling the die and squeezing the bone the amount rolled. Each player has a shovel that they place behind the dog to catch the "doos" before squeezing the bone. Each time the dog poos, you have to refill the bone. Once all the slime is gone, the player with the most "doos" wins. Had I known that the game used slime, I never would have gotten it. I've had to throw out too many items ruined from it to want it in my home anymore. We just try to be extra careful when playing. It comes with two bags, but it only takes one to play. The second bag is for if the first gets ruined. It says on the bag that it's non-toxic, but to still wash hands after touching it. When the game works, it's fun and makes us laugh. We've had lots of trouble getting it to work properly, though. Many times it won't seal just right(I guess) and no amount of squeezing the bone will make anything happen. It warns not to put too much, which we've tried not to do, and to also make sure the bone is pushed all the way in, which we've tried to do. It still won't work for us half the time, though, which makes it frustrating. If the slime ever gets stuck, the game does come with a stick to push it out. It also comes with a puzzle, which is a nice bonus. Overall, it's still a fun game.

Ravensburger Underwater Paradise 9000 Piece Jigsaw Puzzle for Adults - 17807 - Handcrafted Tooling, Durable Blueboard, Every Piece Fits Together Perfectly I know Ravensburger Puzzles are expensive, but worth every penny as they are simply The Best. We have bought them before but never in this huge 9000 piece size. For those not familiar with Ravensburger Puzzles, they are made of the finest sturdy cardboard, hand cut in Germany with such a razor sharp cutter that they leave no cardboard dust and the pieces have an unbelievably tight fit. They have no competitors, as no one comes close to their hand workmanship, bold colors and quality.

The 9000 pieces in this puzzle come in 2 bags- each makes half the puzzle. This makes it so much easier to work on, as we bought 2 pieces of cardboard from our craft store- each a little over 3 feet by 2 feet, to assemble each half on. This half size easily fits on our kitchen table and can be moved easily as well when it's on the cardboard. Included with the 2 puzzle bags is a 3 foot poster of the puzzle to assist you in assembling the beautifully colored pieces. When we were finished with both halves, the full 6 foot 4 inch by 4 1/2 foot puzzle took our breath away! The bold, vivid colors on this large size of all the underwater life looks like a breathtaking work of art just waiting to brighten up a wall in your home.

We decided to put it up on a wall, right behind the children's aquarium- talk about stunning! The only thing we had to decide, is do we use glue to permanently seal it before hanging, or do we seal it tightly in plastic from our local art store, then hang it. The kids said they wanted it in plastic, as they may want to do the puzzle again someday- so it is sealed tightly in plastic against cardboard, framed and hung. If you want this permanently glued, as many people do, all you need to do is buy MasterPieces Puzzle Glue, or any other good puzzle glue and a brush. (I never use the cardboard glue applicators, as the brush is much better). One 5 ounce bottle will seal a 2000 piece puzzle, so you'll need 4 or 5 bottles. You can spread this glue on the front, back or both sides for a permanent bond. It dries clear, so you don't even see the glue.

This 9000 piece high quality Ravensburger Puzzle is worth every cent for the enjoyment of creating a bold, big, beautiful underwater work of art, but what you ultimately gain when you are finished is a gorgeous stunning large wall covering for a bare wall in your home, and that alone is worth the price of these high quality puzzles!

HobbyZone Champ RTF, HBZ4900 This is a great little plane, no question. But I ignored Hobbyzone's recommendation for 14 years old and up. I bought two: one for each of my 9-year-old twin sons, who were hot to fly RC model airplanes. One learned to fly quickly, but the other has been seriously disappointed. And I had to learn quickly how to use styrofoam glue to reattach broken wings, tail parts, motor mounts, etc.

It took me a while to understand how critical the trim really is: a beginner really can't fly a plane that isn't trimmed properly. You can get the trim in the ballpark with visual inspection of the control surfaces, but to get it right you have to fly the plane yourself. When I did that, and touched up the trim, flying became a lot of fun - for one boy. The other boy still can't fly more than a few seconds before landing his plane on its nose. He has just about given up in disgust.

I suspect that in a year or two both boys will have good flying skills. But in the meantime one boy is ready to move up while the other is ready to give up. Bummer!

Colored Pencil Set with Case, 7-Inch, Pack of 72 As an artist, I like to keep a variety of pencils on hand for different projects. I decided to test these out in an adult coloring book (with a fairy) and I am actually very impressed. I had low expectations, a lot of people seem to dislike them, but personally I really like them. My husband works at an art and craft store so I have tried a lot of brands and styles. This pack is a great one for starters or to add to your color palette in pencils. Colored pencils can be blended, but it's a lot easier to have a variety of colors to get the shade you want. I spent about 2 hours coloring this page using only pencils from this pack. There are a few colors I would like to have seen, but over all it's still a very diverse pack. There are a lot of lighter and brighter tons than I have in my other pencils.

The pencils themselves have not given me any trouble. The wood is a little lighter than say the Crayola brand ones, but they sharpen fine and as long as you aren't pressing extremely hard the lead does not break. I pressed fairly hard to blend the trees and none of the pencils broke for me. While this was not an art venture, this page was used for me to test the pencils and I am happy with the results. Before I would color on the page, I used a blank page to scribble a little as it can be hard to differentiate some of the colors from the other shades, but I do this anyway so I am sure about the color I want before I get it on the page and accidentally wreck something.

The colors blended fine, I probably should have gone back and finished shading, but as a test page it worked fine. I mixed this pack in with my other pencils so I can choose from any color I could need. When I started out I used the cheap brand from the craft store and these are much higher quality than those ever were.

I wouldn't consider the plastic thing a case though, it's more like a package. Not easy to use. I put my pencils in a storage tote so I could easily go through and choose the one I need. I may end up buying another pack for my mother down the road, she likes to color and basic pencil sets do not have this variety of colors. The price is extremely competitive as well. I paid almost this much for my set of 48 Crayola pencils.

*I RECEIVED THIS PRODUCT (IN ORDER TO TRY IT AND REVIEW) THIS DOES NOT GUARANTEE A GOOD REVIEW OR CHANGE MY OPINION ON THE PRODUCT, I AM HONEST AND UNBIASED, ALL OPINIONS ON IT ARE MY OWN AND BASED ON THE PRODUCT ITSELF. I HAVE TRIED THIS MYSELF AND EVALUATED IT ACCORDINGLY

Intex Inflatable Jump-O-Lene Playhouse Trampoline Bounce House for Kids Ages 3-6 Pool Red/Yellow, 68-1/2" L x 68-1/2" W x 44" H Like many busy parents who are struggling to work from home during the pandemic while caring for our young kids, I was looking for a toy that would keep my 3-year-old entertained for a few minutes and since he loves jumping and bouncy houses this seemed like a great idea.
This took about 45-60 minutes to inflate and we had to use a blow dryer for the widest opening in addition to an electric pump. It inflated nicely and it did take quite a bit of space in my living room. However, when my son came to try it he became instantly frustrated because the material is very stiff and isn’t bouncy. This is more like an inflatable pool kind of material, only stronger and stiffer. We tried using this several times but my son simply doesn’t enjoy it. Then I tried to return it and they made me a) fit the darn thing in the tiny original box (which of course was impossible) or I wouldn’t get a refund and b) pay for shipping myself. I would’ve had more fun burning $70 something bucks for this piece of junk. I certainly don’t have the time or energy to go through their cumbersome and senseless return process. I don’t recommend it to any parent. I ended up buying a trampoline and my son and I are much happier with that.

Your Barbie-lover will have this doll figured out in a mere moment so going into detail as to how it works is really not necessary.

You get one sheet with only black-and-white lines for an older child to paint and dot. You also get that same design with the main colors pre-printed and you only need to add dots of paint to the white dots in the design. The kit also comes with: 8 acrylic paints (light blue, dark blue, green, yellow-green, yellow, orange, red, purple), 2 fine tip dotters, 1 medium tip dotter, 1 brush, sticky tac (keeps paper flat while painting), 2 cardboard frames with hangers, and instructions. Acrylic paints can dry out quickly, so you may need to add water to the paints to keep them from drying out. Acrylic paints can quickly dry onto clothing and not come out, so you'll want to wear a painting smock. Wash dotters, brush (and work surface) before the paint dries if you intend to reuse them. The "dotters" are foam rounds on the end of a handle, and they create somewhat raised paint dots on the design sheets. It's a fun idea with colorful paints, but it is kind of simple so probably for younger kids rather than teenagers or older.

text_fidelity_a:
Wonder Forge Marvel I Can Do That! Game We also have this game in the Dr. Seuss theme, and they're both fun. They're very similar in both cards and directions, but this one is great for little fans of Marvel.

There's a note on the directions page to let you know it's fine to customize the rules for your family. (We tend to do that anyway, but it's a great reminder!) There are 3 stacks of numbered/colored cards(1-red, 2-blue, 3-green). The player turns over one card from each stack. They'll tell the player what to do with which objects. For example, the first card will tell you to "Do a push-up". The second card: "with Captain Marvel's energy ball", and the third card: "on your head". Some tasks are harder than others! Each card will get a certain amount of stars. (At the end of the game, the players will add the stars up. The player with the most wins.) If your child thinks he/she can do the specified task, they will say, "I Can Do That!" If not, they can exchange a card at a time until they feel they can do the task. One of my children was given the task of "Crab walk under the portal, with Spider-Man's web, between your elbows". None of us were talented enough to do that, so he picked again. This is also a great escape route for the shyer(or younger) little ones. Some things will be less embarrassing or more doable for them than others.

There are also "Battle" cards. If one of those are drawn, then any other cards drawn will be put back in the mix. The player will then try to knock down the Green Goblin card with the object specified on the card. If the task is completed, the card is set aside. If not, the player has to put that card in his/her pile as a reminder to discard 2 cards before counting stars at the end of the game. (That way, they can discard to 2 with the lowest number of stars.)

While it may get old with what the players do, it does create a variety of mix and match tasks. The cards are constantly being shuffled. The game ends when all the cards are gone.

This is a great game for when movement is needed. It's not one that the players just sit around and play. The players have to get up and move around. There's also a nice variety of types of objects. There's a plastic block that will need to be filled with air, along with a ball(that's already aired up). There's foam items and thick cardboard objects(Green Goblin and Captain America's shield). My biggest complaint is the "portal". This isn't the sturdiest of things. It's hard to get it to stand up straight, mainly because it has to be rolled up a bit to fit in the box. It makes it hard to get under at times. The bigger/older the child, the harder it will be to crawl under it, either way. This is definitely a game for littler/younger people. Also, I fear that the block won't last long, since objects that require air don't make it too long around my home, in general. (For it to fit back in the box after each game, the air will have to be released. That means you'll have to blow it up before each game. It's not huge, so it's not the biggest deal. Particularly if used in a classroom setting, though, germs/cleaning wipes would be something to put into consideration.)

My children(3, 5, and a tiny 8) have really enjoyed playing this game, though!
text_fidelity_b: Wonder Forge Marvel I Can Do That! Game

text_fidelity_a:
The Secret Life of Pets - Snowball Walking Talking Pets Figure This is a 'cute' little toy. I like the expression on his face. We've had fun playing with it for the past couple weeks.

Some things that you might want to know about it if you're considering buying one.

The instructions suggest replacing the two AAA batteries when you take the figure out of the package - the two that come in it are for 'in-store' demonstration purposes. Opening the battery compartment I found that the supplied batteries are pretty decent alkaline ones. Still, I replaced the ones in mine as I hate it when batteries go dead in a device and then leak. Something to maybe mention - the battery compartment is secured with a screw, so that small hands can't get into it.

The tail on the rabbit acts as the on/off switch. There are three setting - On, Off, and Demo. In the demonstration mode the figure talks and the wheels turn for a few seconds and then stops. When in the On position, the figure says a phrase - the wheels go for awhile and then it stops and repeats the cycle. The figure has three wheels - two fixed wheels seem to drive it's motion and a third rotates to make the figure go in different directions. Our rabbit seems to have a habit of finding the nearest corner and parking itself in it. The figure's eyes move a bit when it's in running around (although it's hard to see with the way it's eyes are set).

The figure comes with a separate carrot prop. Which the rabbit is suppose to hold in it's one hand - ours kept dropping his. So I took a piece of the white string that had secured the toy to the package and tied the carrot to his hand- you can't really even see it.

The rabbit talks, and I know it's suppose to be Kevin Hart doing a 'cartoon' voice - but it's really hard to understand what it's suppose to be saying. Hopefully when the movie comes out the phrases will be more recognizable.

All in all I like this figure and I'm looking forward to seeing the movie.
text_fidelity_b: The Secret Life of Pets - Snowball Walking Talking Pets Figure

text_fidelity_a:
Scientific Explorer Disgusting Anatomy Brain My boys(3, 5, and 7) had fun with this kit, overall, but there's really not much to it.

Basically, you mix up cornstarch, gelatin(both provided), and water, through various steps, and then pour it into the provided molds. This project has to be done in several steps, with waiting periods in between. With my children being so young, the wait was annoying. Thankfully, we did the project on a day that it was beautiful outside, and there was plenty of play in between, so it could have been worse.

After the brain/eye has set up in the mold, you'll dump it out, and paint it. You get paint(food coloring) in the kit, and can mix it up to what colors you want. My children were disappointed that they couldn't get the colors to look as bright as they do in the pictures. I even helped with this attempt. The colors were just very dull, and our brain didn't look anywhere near how bright it was shown to be. I'd recommend using real paint, as opposed to food coloring. I think the results will be better.

The molds are reusable, so as long as you don't mind buying more gelatin and cornstarch, you can make as many brains and eye balls as you'd like.

Overall, this is a fun little experiment if you're studying brains or eyes. It's very simple, though, despite the several steps, which make it time consuming.
text_fidelity_b: Scientific Explorer Disgusting Anatomy Brain
